title: ⭐ Practice: the word, the form and the mark

questions.prompt: The word "assistance" belongs in exactly one of these four gaps. Which sentence needs it?

options.text: Every ___ of the household knows what the others expect of them.
Serious problems ___ the moment one person carries every role.
Working mothers often manage the house with very little ___.
Nobody can ___ a role that nobody has explained to him.

questions.explanation: assistance means help, and only one gap is waiting for a noun that names help: with very little assistance. The word very little also settles it, because it stands in front of things you cannot count, and help is one of them. The gap after Every needs member, the word for a person who belongs to the family, and member can be counted. The gap after Serious problems needs arise, the verb that means to come into being. The gap after Nobody can needs fulfil, the verb for carrying a role out completely.

questions.prompt: Complete this list of chores: "Oussama sets the table, waters the plants and ___ the rubbish."
questions.explanation: English marries take out to the household waste, and the pair has to be learnt whole: he "takes out" the rubbish. "brings up" is a real phrasal verb, but it means raising a child or raising a subject in a conversation, and neither is a chore. "puts down" means setting an object on a surface, which is the opposite journey: the rubbish is meant to leave the house. "takes off" means removing a garment, or leaving the ground as a plane does, and neither has anything to do with a bin.

questions.prompt: A crossword clue is written as a family: "charity (noun) … (adjective)". Which word fills the squares?
questions.explanation: The little words in brackets say that the clue starts from a noun and asks for the adjective of the same family, and the adjective English builds on charity is "charitable": a charitable association, a charitable act. "charities" is the plural of the noun, and the clue has already handed you the noun. "charitably" is the adverb, the form that follows a verb, as in she gave charitably. "charitive" copies the -ive of active and supportive onto a word that refuses it, and no such English word exists.

questions.prompt: Complete with the phrasal verb that carries the meaning printed in brackets: "I am ___ Mr Chedly Ayari. Do you know which floor he works on?" (seek somebody)
questions.explanation: look for means seeking somebody or something you cannot find, which is exactly the meaning in brackets and exactly why the speaker is asking for a floor number: "looking for". "looking after" is one particle away and a whole job away: it means taking care of somebody, and you do not take care of a man you have not met yet. "gazing at" means looking fixedly, and nobody can gaze at a person who is not there. "picking up" means lifting somebody or something from the ground.

questions.prompt: In the sentence "You ___ see a doctor." the verb see is printed with no to in front of it. Which of these four words can stand in the gap exactly as it is?
questions.explanation: "must" is a modal and is followed by the bare verb, so You must see a doctor is complete as it stands. "have" demands its to: you have to see a doctor. "need" demands one as well, because in a plain statement like this one it is an ordinary verb: you need to see a doctor, which is the form the printed sentence is really asking for. The modal need does exist, but it lives in negatives and questions — needn't, need I say more? — never in a plain affirmative. "ought" is the one modal that keeps a to after it: you ought to see a doctor.

questions.prompt: Marwa writes in her diary: "I wish I had my own room." What does her sentence tell you about her situation today?

options.text: She has her own room and is happy with it.
She had her own room and then lost it.
She will have her own room next year.
She has not got her own room.

questions.explanation: After wish, a past form does not look back at the past: it describes what is not true now. The diary therefore says that today "She has not got her own room." "She had her own room and then lost it." reads had as an ordinary past, but to look that far back English needs I wish I had had my own room. "She has her own room and is happy with it." turns a regret into contentment, and nobody wishes for what they already have. "She will have her own room next year." turns it into a plan, whereas wish states a lack and never a date.
